walkthroughs.body_html:
Chemistry of the Environment — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Chemistry of the Environment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Chemistry of the Environment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.

mcqs.q: Why can an endothermic reaction still be spontaneous?
options: If the entropy increase (TΔS) is large enough to outweigh the positive ΔH, ΔG can still be negative.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Endothermic reactions are never spontaneous because they require energy input.
